questions.q: Why does this lesson's troubleshooting method insist on reproducing the problem with evidence before forming a hypothesis?
options: Because Salesforce requires a support ticket number before any debugging can begin
Because a vague description risks diagnosing and "fixing" the wrong cause, especially since a limit exception's line number often points at the unlucky operation rather than the real root cause
Because debug logs cannot be captured unless the exact error message is already known
Reproduction is optional and mainly useful for documentation purposes, not diagnosis
questions.explain: Skipping reproduction and jumping to an assumed cause risks fixing a symptom (the operation that happened to cross a limit) while leaving the actual root cause — often unrelated automation sharing the same transaction — untouched.

questions.q: What distinguishes a "hard failure" from a "soft failure" in this lesson's terms?
options: A hard failure only happens in production, while a soft failure only happens in sandboxes
A hard failure is any error message in English, while a soft failure is any error in another language
There is no real difference; both terms describe the exact same outcome
A hard failure throws a governor limit exception and rolls back entirely; a soft failure completes successfully but consumes an unhealthy share of its limit budget
questions.explain: A hard failure is an explicit thrown exception that rolls back the transaction. A soft failure succeeds but is quietly using far more of its governor limit budget than it should, which is dangerous precisely because nothing visibly broke.

questions.q: Why is a soft failure arguably more dangerous to miss than a hard failure?
options: Because soft failures always cause permanent data corruption, unlike hard failures
Because soft failures are impossible to detect with any tool covered in this course

Because the transaction appears to work fine, so unless someone actually reads the CUMULATIVE_LIMIT_USAGE numbers, the problem goes unnoticed until future growth or added automation pushes it into an actual exception
Because soft failures only occur in asynchronous Apex, never in synchronous transactions
questions.explain: A hard failure announces itself immediately with a thrown exception. A soft failure succeeds silently, so it's easy to overlook until something else (more data, more automation) eventually tips it over the edge into a real exception.

questions.q: In step 3 of the troubleshooting method (locating where time or limit usage actually went), which Chapter 2 tool or log section is specifically referenced?
options: The Logs tab's Execution Overview and the debug log's CUMULATIVE_LIMIT_USAGE block
The Query Plan tool exclusively, since it's the only tool that reports timing
Event Monitoring exclusively, since debug logs cannot show elapsed time
The Salesforce Setup Audit Trail
questions.explain: Step 3 specifically points to the Execution Overview (for which category dominates elapsed time) and CUMULATIVE_LIMIT_USAGE (for which specific limit is closest to its ceiling), both covered in Lessons 7 and 8.

questions.q: Why does the method insist on testing a hypothesis in isolation (step 5) before applying a fix (step 6)?
options: Because Salesforce requires all fixes to be tested in a separate sandbox org by policy
To confirm the suspected cause is actually responsible before changing production code, rather than assuming the first plausible-looking explanation is correct
Because isolated testing automatically applies the fix for you once confirmed
Isolation testing is only relevant for asynchronous Apex, not synchronous code
questions.explain: Testing the specific hypothesis in isolation (via Execute Anonymous or the Query Plan tool) confirms the suspected cause before any production change is made, avoiding wasted effort fixing something that wasn't actually the problem.
